hs_math_t09_st01.title: Geometric definitions and notation
hs_math_t09_st01.overview: Euclidean geometry uses precise terms and symbols to describe points, lines, planes, angles and their relationships. Correct notation tells a reader exactly which object or part of a diagram is meant.

key_concepts.definition: The objects from which diagrams are built.
details: A **point** marks an exact position and has no length, width or thickness. It is named with a capital letter, such as $A$.
A **line** is straight and extends without end in both directions. The line through $A$ and $B$ is written $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$.
A **line segment** has two endpoints and a measurable length: $\overline{AB}$.
A **ray** has one endpoint and extends forever in one direction: $\overrightarrow{AB}$ begins at $A$ and passes through $B$.
A **plane** is a flat two-dimensional surface extending without boundary. Three non-collinear points can determine a plane.
An **angle** is formed by two rays with a common endpoint (the vertex). In $\angle ABC$, the vertex is $B$.

key_concepts.definition: How geometric objects may be positioned.
details: Points are **collinear** if they lie on one straight line.
Objects are **coplanar** if they lie in one plane.
In three-dimensional geometry, **skew lines** are non-parallel lines that do not intersect because they are not coplanar.

key_concepts.definition: Markings communicate stated relationships.
details: Matching tick marks on segments indicate equal lengths. Different tick-mark patterns denote different equality groups.
Matching arrow marks on lines indicate parallel lines.
Matching angle arcs indicate equal angle measures. A small square at a vertex indicates a right angle ($90^\circ$).
A diagram is not assumed to be drawn to scale unless the problem says so; use the given labels and markings.

worked_examples.problem: In triangle $ABC$, points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are vertices. A ray starts at $B$ and passes through $C$. Write the ray notation and identify its endpoint.
solution_steps: The first letter in ray notation is its endpoint.
The ray starts at $B$ and passes through $C$, so it is written $\overrightarrow{BC}$.

worked_examples.problem: If $M$ is the midpoint of segment $\overline{AB}$ and $AM=7$ cm, find $AB$.
solution_steps: A midpoint divides a segment into two equal lengths, so $AM=MB=7$ cm.
Add the two parts: $AB=AM+MB=7+7=14$ cm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a line, ray and segment as interchangeable.
common_mistakes.correction: A line has no endpoints, a ray has one endpoint, and a segment has two endpoints and a finite length.

common_mistakes.mistake: Naming an angle with the vertex in the wrong position.
common_mistakes.correction: In $\angle ABC$, the middle letter $B$ is the vertex. Check the order before using an angle in a proof.

quick_summary: A line extends in both directions; a ray has one endpoint; a segment has two.
The middle letter in a three-letter angle name is its vertex.
Collinear means on one line; coplanar means in one plane; skew lines are non-coplanar and non-intersecting.

hs_math_t09_st02.title: Angle properties
hs_math_t09_st02.overview: Angles formed by intersecting lines and rays obey fixed relationships. These properties can be used to calculate unknown angles and justify each step in a short Euclidean argument.

key_concepts.definition: Angles that share a vertex and a side.
details: **Adjacent angles** share a common vertex and one common arm, and their interiors do not overlap.
A **linear pair** is a pair of adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line. Their measures add to $180^\circ$.

key_concepts.definition: Pairs classified by their angle sum.
details: **Complementary angles** have measures that add to $90^\circ$. They need not be adjacent.
**Supplementary angles** have measures that add to $180^\circ$. They need not be adjacent; a linear pair is a special adjacent case.

key_concepts.concept: Vertically opposite angles and angles around a point
key_concepts.definition: Relationships at an intersection.
details: When two straight lines intersect, each pair of **vertically opposite angles** has equal measures.
Angles around a point make one complete turn and have a total measure of $360^\circ$.
A linear pair and vertically opposite-angle facts can be used together to determine all four angles formed by two intersecting lines.

worked_examples.problem: Two straight lines intersect. A pair of vertically opposite angles measures $(3x+10)^\circ$ and $(5x-30)^\circ$. Find all four angles.
solution_steps: Vertically opposite angles are equal: $3x+10=5x-30$.
Add 30 and subtract $3x$: $40=2x$, so $x=20$.
The first angle is $3(20)+10=70^\circ$. Its vertically opposite angle is also $70^\circ$.
Each adjacent angle forms a linear pair with $70^\circ$, so it is $180^\circ-70^\circ=110^\circ$.

worked_examples.problem: Two complementary angles are in the ratio $2:3$. Find their measures.
solution_steps: Let the angles be $2x$ and $3x$. Complementary angles sum to $90^\circ$.
So $2x+3x=90$, giving $x=18$.
The angles are $2(18)=36^\circ$ and $3(18)=54^\circ$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming all supplementary angles must touch.
common_mistakes.correction: Supplementary angles only need to sum to $180^\circ$. A linear pair is supplementary and also adjacent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing vertical opposite angles with adjacent angles.
common_mistakes.correction: Vertically opposite angles are across the intersection and equal. Adjacent angles share a side; a linear pair sums to $180^\circ$.

quick_summary: Complementary angles sum to $90^\circ$; supplementary angles sum to $180^\circ$.
A linear pair is adjacent and sums to $180^\circ$.
Vertically opposite angles are equal; angles around a point sum to $360^\circ$.

hs_math_t09_st03.title: Parallel lines and transversals
hs_math_t09_st03.overview: A transversal crossing two parallel lines creates pairs of equal and supplementary angles. The converse properties allow the same angle relationships to be used as evidence that two lines are parallel.

key_concepts.definition: Angles occupying corresponding or opposite positions.
details: **Corresponding angles** occupy the same relative position at the two intersections and are equal when the lines are parallel.
**Alternate interior angles** lie between the parallel lines on opposite sides of the transversal and are equal.
**Alternate exterior angles** lie outside the parallel lines on opposite sides of the transversal and are equal.

key_concepts.definition: Interior angles on the same side of the transversal.
details: Co-interior (same-side interior) angles lie between the two lines and on the same side of the transversal. When the lines are parallel, they are supplementary and sum to $180^\circ$.

key_concepts.definition: Proving parallelism from angle information.
details: If a pair of corresponding angles is equal, the two lines are parallel.
If a pair of alternate interior angles is equal, the two lines are parallel.
If a pair of co-interior angles sums to $180^\circ$, the two lines are parallel.
Use the converse only when the angle positions are correctly identified; an angle pair with a different relationship does not establish parallelism.

formulas.name: Corresponding and alternate angle relationships
formulas.equation: $$\text{Corresponding angles equal; alternate interior angles equal}$$

worked_examples.problem: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. A pair of co-interior angles measures $(3x+20)^\circ$ and $(2x+10)^\circ$. Find $x$ and the angles.
solution_steps: Co-interior angles between parallel lines sum to $180^\circ$.
Combine like terms: $5x+30=180$, so $5x=150$ and $x=30$.
The angles are $3(30)+20=110^\circ$ and $2(30)+10=70^\circ$.

worked_examples.problem: A transversal creates alternate interior angles of $68^\circ$ and $68^\circ$ on two lines. What can be concluded?
solution_steps: The two alternate interior angles are equal.
By the converse of the alternate-interior-angle theorem, the two lines are parallel.

common_mistakes.mistake: Setting co-interior angles equal.
common_mistakes.correction: For parallel lines, corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are equal. Co-interior angles sum to $180^\circ$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using parallel-line angle rules without establishing parallelism.
common_mistakes.correction: First check that the lines are stated to be parallel or that a valid converse condition has been proved.

quick_summary: Corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are equal for parallel lines.
Co-interior angles sum to $180^\circ$.
The converse of these relationships can be used to prove two lines parallel.

hs_math_t09_st04.title: Triangle properties
hs_math_t09_st04.overview: Triangle properties are developed through the angle-sum and exterior-angle theorems, relationships between side lengths and opposite angles, and the triangle inequality. These results support deductions and formal proofs rather than simple angle identification.

key_concepts.definition: The angle relationships in every plane triangle.
details: The three interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$.
An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent (remote) interior angles.
An exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle form a linear pair and therefore sum to $180^\circ$.

A proof of the angle-sum theorem can be made by drawing a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side. Alternate interior angles reproduce the other two interior angles along a straight line, whose angle sum is $180^\circ$. The exterior-angle theorem then follows from the triangle angle sum and a linear pair.

key_concepts.definition: Comparing sides and their opposite angles.
details: In any triangle, the longer side lies opposite the larger angle, and the shorter side lies opposite the smaller angle.
Equal sides are opposite equal angles (the isosceles-triangle theorem). Conversely, equal angles are opposite equal sides.

key_concepts.definition: The condition for three lengths to form a triangle.
details: The sum of the lengths of any two sides must be greater than the length of the remaining side.
When side lengths are ordered $a\le b\le c$, it is sufficient to check $a+b>c$.
For example, lengths 3, 4 and 10 cannot form a triangle because $3+4$ is not greater than 10.

worked_examples.problem: An exterior angle is $(5x+10)^\circ$. Its two remote interior angles are $(2x+20)^\circ$ and $(x+30)^\circ$. Find $x$ and all three interior angles.
solution_steps: By the exterior-angle theorem, $5x+10=(2x+20)+(x+30)$.
Simplify: $5x+10=3x+50$, so $2x=40$ and $x=20$.
The remote interior angles are $2(20)+20=60^\circ$ and $20+30=50^\circ$.
The interior angle adjacent to the exterior angle is $180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ$. Check: $60+50+70=180$.

worked_examples.problem: Can lengths 6 cm, 8 cm and 15 cm form a triangle?
solution_steps: The two shorter lengths must add to more than the longest length.
$6+8=14$, and $14$ is not greater than $15$.
The triangle inequality fails, so a triangle with these side lengths cannot be formed.
worked_examples.final_answer: No. The lengths do not satisfy the triangle inequality.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming any three positive lengths form a triangle.
common_mistakes.correction: Check all three triangle inequalities; with the lengths ordered, check that the two shorter sides sum to more than the longest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the adjacent interior angle in the exterior-angle theorem.
common_mistakes.correction: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, not the interior angle next to it.

quick_summary: Interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
Longer sides lie opposite larger angles; equal sides lie opposite equal angles.
The sum of any two side lengths must exceed the third.

hs_math_t09_st05.title: Congruence of triangles
hs_math_t09_st05.overview: Congruent triangles have the same shape and size. A valid congruence criterion proves that their corresponding sides and angles match, allowing further results to be established using corresponding parts of congruent triangles.

key_concepts.definition: Sufficient information to prove two triangles congruent.
details: **SSS:** all three pairs of corresponding sides are equal.
**SAS:** two pairs of corresponding sides and the included angle are equal.
**ASA:** two pairs of corresponding angles and the included side are equal.
**AAS:** two pairs of corresponding angles and a corresponding non-included side are equal.
**RHS (or HL):** in right triangles, the hypotenuse and one corresponding leg are equal.

key_concepts.definition: Using the order of vertices correctly.
details: Write triangle names in corresponding order. In $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle DEF$, the correspondence is $A\leftrightarrow D$, $B\leftrightarrow E$, and $C\leftrightarrow F$.
**CPCTC** means corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent. Use it only after congruence has been established.

key_concepts.concept: Conditions that do not prove congruence
key_concepts.definition: Recognising insufficient information.
details: **AAA** establishes similarity (same shape) but not equal size, so it does not prove congruence.
**SSA** is not a general congruence criterion. In some cases it can produce two different triangles; do not treat it as a valid general test.

worked_examples.problem: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, diagonal $AC$ divides it into two triangles. Given $AB=CD$ and $BC=DA$, prove $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle CDA$.
solution_steps: The given equalities are $AB=CD$ and $BC=DA$.
The triangles share side $AC$, so $AC=CA$ by the reflexive property.
The three matching side pairs are $AB=CD$, $BC=DA$ and $AC=CA$.
Therefore $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle CDA$ by SSS. The order shows $A\leftrightarrow C$, $B\leftrightarrow D$ and $C\leftrightarrow A$.

worked_examples.problem: Two right triangles have equal hypotenuses of 13 cm and one pair of corresponding legs of 5 cm. What criterion proves them congruent?
solution_steps: Both triangles are right triangles.
Their hypotenuses are equal and one pair of corresponding legs is equal.
These are exactly the conditions of RHS (also called HL) congruence.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the angle in the wrong position for SAS.
common_mistakes.correction: For SAS, the known angle must be included between the two known corresponding sides.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating AAA or SSA as a general congruence test.
common_mistakes.correction: AAA proves similarity, not congruence. SSA is ambiguous in general and is not a valid universal congruence criterion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using CPCTC before proving congruence.
common_mistakes.correction: First establish congruence with a valid criterion, then state corresponding equal parts.

quick_summary: The main criteria are SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS/HL.
Keep the corresponding vertex order consistent.
AAA proves similarity, while SSA is not a general congruence criterion.
Use CPCTC only after proving the triangles congruent.

hs_math_t09_st06.title: Similarity of triangles
hs_math_t09_st06.overview: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding side lengths. Similarity criteria allow a proof of equal shape, while scale factors connect corresponding lengths, perimeters and areas.

key_concepts.definition: Ways to prove two triangles have the same shape.
details: **AA:** two pairs of corresponding angles are equal; the third pair is then equal by the triangle angle sum.
**SSS similarity:** all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
**SAS similarity:** two pairs of corresponding sides are proportional and the included angles are equal.

key_concepts.definition: A common multiplier between matching lengths.
details: Match corresponding vertices and sides before forming ratios. If a side in the image triangle is compared with its matching side in the original triangle, the scale factor is $k=\text{image length}/\text{original length}$.
Corresponding side lengths, heights and perimeters scale by $k$. If $k>1$, the image is an enlargement; if $0<k<1$, it is a reduction.

key_concepts.definition: How the area changes when lengths are scaled.
details: Areas scale by the square of the linear scale factor: $k^2$.
If corresponding sides are in the ratio $2:5$, the larger-to-smaller area ratio is $2^2:5^2=4:25$.

worked_examples.problem: Triangle A has sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm. Triangle B is similar and its longest side is 21 cm. Find the shortest side of triangle B.
solution_steps: The longest sides correspond: 7 cm in A and 21 cm in B.
The scale factor from A to B is $k=21/7=3$.
The shortest side in A is 4 cm, so the matching side in B is $4\times3=12$ cm.

worked_examples.problem: Two similar triangles have corresponding side ratio (small to large) $2:5$. If the smaller triangle has area 16 cm², find the larger area.
solution_steps: The linear scale factor from small to large is $k=5/2$.
The area scale factor is $k^2=(5/2)^2=25/4$.
Larger area $=16\times25/4=4\times25=100$ cm².

worked_examples.problem: In $\triangle ABC$, points $D$ and $E$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$, and $DE\parallel BC$. If $AD=4$ cm, $AB=10$ cm and $AE=6$ cm, find $AC$.
solution_steps: Because $DE\parallel BC$, corresponding angles are equal, so $\triangle ADE\sim\triangle ABC$ by AA.
Corresponding sides are proportional: $AD/AB=AE/AC$.
Substitute: $4/10=6/AC$. Cross-multiply: $4AC=60$.
Therefore $AC=15$ cm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing non-corresponding sides.
common_mistakes.correction: Write the vertex correspondence first, then compare matching sides in the same order.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the linear scale factor for area.
common_mistakes.correction: Lengths and perimeter scale by $k$; area scales by $k^2$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming two triangles are similar because they look alike.
common_mistakes.correction: Prove similarity using AA, SSS similarity or SAS similarity.

quick_summary: Prove similarity using AA, SSS or SAS.
Corresponding side lengths and perimeters scale by $k$.
Corresponding areas scale by $k^2$.
Parallel lines often create similar triangles by AA.

hs_math_t09_st07.title: Quadrilaterals and polygons
hs_math_t09_st07.overview: Quadrilaterals and polygons are classified by their side and angle properties. Theorems about parallel sides, equal sides, angles and diagonals allow properties of each shape to be justified and applied.

key_concepts.definition: Quadrilaterals with related side, angle and diagonal properties.
details: A **parallelogram** has both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary, and the diagonals bisect each other.
A **rectangle** is a parallelogram with four right angles. Its diagonals are equal and bisect each other.
A **rhombus** is a parallelogram with four equal sides. Its diagonals bisect each other at right angles and bisect opposite angles.
A **square** is both a rectangle and a rhombus: it has four equal sides, four right angles, and equal perpendicular diagonals.

key_concepts.definition: Trapeziums/trapezoids and kites.
details: A **trapezium/trapezoid** has exactly one pair of parallel opposite sides under the convention used in these notes. Terminology varies between countries; some textbooks use “trapezoid” for a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides.
A **kite** has two distinct pairs of equal adjacent sides. Its diagonals are perpendicular, and one diagonal (the symmetry diagonal) bisects the other.

key_concepts.definition: Equal sides and angles, and connections between non-adjacent vertices.
details: A **regular polygon** has all sides equal and all interior angles equal. A rectangle is not regular unless it is a square.
A **diagonal** joins two non-adjacent vertices of a polygon. From each vertex of an $n$-gon, $n-3$ diagonals can be drawn; each diagonal is counted from both endpoints, so the total is $n(n-3)/2$.

worked_examples.problem: How many diagonals can be drawn inside a nonagon (9-sided polygon)?
solution_steps: A nonagon has $n=9$ vertices.

worked_examples.problem: A parallelogram has one interior angle of $68^\circ$. Find the other three interior angles.
solution_steps: Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal, so the opposite angle is $68^\circ$.
Adjacent angles are supplementary: $180^\circ-68^\circ=112^\circ$.
The remaining angle opposite $112^\circ$ is also $112^\circ$.

worked_examples.problem: In parallelogram $ABCD$, diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $O$. Prove that $AO=CO$ and $BO=DO$.
solution_steps: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel and equal, so $AB\parallel CD$ and $AB=CD$.
Because $AB\parallel CD$, alternate interior angles give $\angle BAO=\angle DCO$ and $\angle ABO=\angle CDO$.
Thus $\triangle ABO\cong\triangle CDO$ by ASA.
By CPCTC, $AO=CO$ and $BO=DO$.
worked_examples.final_answer: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a rhombus has equal diagonals.
common_mistakes.correction: A rhombus has perpendicular diagonals that bisect each other, but they are not generally equal. Equal diagonals are guaranteed in a rectangle and a square.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking a rectangle is a regular polygon.
common_mistakes.correction: A regular polygon must have all sides and all angles equal. A rectangle with unequal adjacent sides is not regular.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the trapezium/trapezoid names as universal.
common_mistakes.correction: Terminology differs by region. State the parallel-side definition being used in a problem.

quick_summary: A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal; its diagonals bisect each other.
A rectangle has equal diagonals; a rhombus has perpendicular diagonals; a square has both properties.
A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
The number of diagonals in an $n$-gon is $n(n-3)/2$.

hs_math_t09_st08.title: Interior and exterior angles of polygons
hs_math_t09_st08.overview: The interior and exterior angle sums of polygons can be derived by dividing a polygon into triangles and by considering the total turn made around its boundary. Regular polygons have equal interior and exterior angles, making individual angles calculable.

key_concepts.definition: Triangulating a polygon.
details: Drawing diagonals from one vertex of a convex $n$-gon divides it into $n-2$ non-overlapping triangles.
Each triangle has angle sum $180^\circ$, so the polygon interior-angle sum is $(n-2)180^\circ$.
For a quadrilateral this gives $(4-2)180^\circ=360^\circ$.

key_concepts.definition: One complete turn around a convex polygon.
details: Taking one exterior angle at each vertex in the same direction gives a total turn of $360^\circ$.
Thus the sum of one exterior angle at each vertex of any convex polygon is $360^\circ$.

key_concepts.definition: Finding one interior or exterior angle.
details: In a regular $n$-gon, each exterior angle is $360^\circ/n$.
Each interior angle is $180^\circ-360^\circ/n$, equivalently $(n-2)180^\circ/n$.
The number of sides can be found from a regular polygon exterior angle: $n=360^\circ/E$.

worked_examples.problem: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $150^\circ$. How many sides does it have?
solution_steps: The corresponding exterior angle is $180^\circ-150^\circ=30^\circ$.
The exterior angles sum to $360^\circ$.
The number of sides is $n=360/30=12$.

worked_examples.problem: Find the sum of the interior angles of a 9-sided polygon.
solution_steps: For $n=9$, use $S=(n-2)180^\circ$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using $n\times180^\circ$ for the interior sum.
common_mistakes.correction: A convex $n$-gon divides into $n-2$ triangles from one vertex, so use $(n-2)180^\circ$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the exterior-angle sum increases with the number of sides.
common_mistakes.correction: One exterior angle at each vertex always sums to $360^\circ$ for a convex polygon.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using $360^\circ/n$ for an irregular polygon.
common_mistakes.correction: Each exterior angle is $360^\circ/n$ only when the polygon is regular.

quick_summary: Interior-angle sum: $(n-2)180^\circ$.
The exterior angles, one at each vertex in the same direction, sum to $360^\circ$.
For a regular polygon, each exterior angle is $360^\circ/n$ and each interior angle is $180^\circ-360^\circ/n$.

hs_math_t09_st09.title: Circle geometry
hs_math_t09_st09.overview: A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance from a fixed point called the centre. This lesson establishes the vocabulary and basic relationships needed for the chord, angle and tangent theorems that follow.

key_concepts.definition: The principal parts of a circle.
details: The **centre** is the fixed point from which all points on the circumference are the same distance.
A **radius** is a segment from the centre to the circumference. All radii of the same circle are equal.
A **diameter** is a chord passing through the centre. Its length is twice the radius: $d=2r$. A diameter is the longest chord of a circle.

key_concepts.definition: Straight and curved parts of a circle.
details: A **chord** is a line segment joining two points on the circumference. A diameter is a special chord that passes through the centre.
An **arc** is a connected portion of the circumference between two points. Two endpoints determine a minor arc and a major arc (unless they are endpoints of a diameter, which determine semicircles).

key_concepts.definition: Regions enclosed by radii, arcs and chords.
details: A **sector** is a region bounded by two radii and the included arc.
A **segment** is a region bounded by a chord and its corresponding arc.
Do not confuse the circumference (the curved boundary) with the area (the region inside the circle). Detailed circumference and area calculations belong with measurement.

worked_examples.problem: A circular plate has radius 8 cm. Find its diameter.
solution_steps: The diameter is twice the radius.
$d=2r=2\times8=16$ cm.

worked_examples.problem: A chord is a segment joining two points on a circle. Is every chord a diameter? Explain.
solution_steps: A diameter is a special chord that passes through the centre.
A chord that does not pass through the centre is not a diameter.
worked_examples.final_answer: No. Every diameter is a chord, but not every chord is a diameter.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling every chord a diameter.
common_mistakes.correction: A diameter is only a chord that passes through the centre.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing a sector with a segment.
common_mistakes.correction: A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc; a segment is bounded by a chord and an arc.

quick_summary: All radii in a circle are equal.
A diameter passes through the centre and is twice the radius.
A chord joins two points on the circumference; an arc is part of the circumference.
A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc; a segment by a chord and an arc.

hs_math_t09_st10.title: Chords, arcs and sectors
hs_math_t09_st10.overview: Chords, arcs and sectors are linked by the centre and the angles they subtend. Equal chords and equal arcs have matching relationships, and perpendicular distances from the centre provide a useful way to compare or calculate chord lengths.

key_concepts.definition: Matching chord and arc sizes in the same circle (or congruent circles).
details: Equal chords in the same circle (or congruent circles) subtend equal minor arcs.
Equal minor arcs in the same circle (or congruent circles) have equal corresponding chords.
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and chords equidistant from the centre are equal.

key_concepts.concept: Perpendicular from the centre to a chord
key_concepts.definition: A right-angle line from the centre bisects the chord.
details: A perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
Conversely, the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
The radius to an endpoint, the perpendicular distance from the centre and half the chord form a right triangle. Pythagoras can be used to find a missing length.

key_concepts.definition: How a central angle describes a sector.
details: A sector is larger when its central angle is larger in the same circle. Equal central angles in the same circle determine equal sectors and equal corresponding arcs.
Detailed arc-length and sector-area calculations are treated in the measurement curriculum; they are not developed here.

worked_examples.problem: A perpendicular is drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord. The radius is 13 cm and the distance from the centre to the chord is 5 cm. Find the full chord length.
solution_steps: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so the right triangle has hypotenuse 13 cm, one leg 5 cm and the other leg half the chord, $x$.
By Pythagoras, $x^2+5^2=13^2$.
The full chord is $2x=24$ cm.

worked_examples.problem: Two chords of the same circle are equal. What can be said about their minor arcs and their distances from the centre?
solution_steps: Equal chords in the same circle subtend equal minor arcs.
Equal chords are also equidistant from the centre.
worked_examples.final_answer: Their minor arcs are equal, and their perpendicular distances from the centre are equal.

worked_examples.problem: In a circle with centre $O$, equal chords $AB$ and $CD$ have perpendiculars $OM$ and $ON$ to them. Explain why the chords are equidistant from the centre.
solution_steps: A perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, so $AM=AB/2$ and $CN=CD/2$.
Since $AB=CD$, their halves are equal: $AM=CN$.
Also, $OA=OC$ because they are radii, and $\angle OMA=\angle ONC=90^\circ$.
The right triangles $OMA$ and $ONC$ are congruent by RHS, so $OM=ON$ by CPCTC.
worked_examples.final_answer: Equal chords in the same circle are equidistant from the centre.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the radius as the half-chord.
common_mistakes.correction: The radius is the hypotenuse of the right triangle. The chord is twice the other leg, which is the half-chord.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming equal chords have different distances from the centre.
common_mistakes.correction: Equal chords in the same circle are equidistant from the centre; the converse is also true.

quick_summary: Equal chords subtend equal minor arcs, and conversely.
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre.
A perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord.
For a chord problem, use $x^2+d^2=r^2$ and double the half-chord.

hs_math_t09_st11.title: Angles subtended by chords
hs_math_t09_st11.overview: Angles at the centre and circumference of a circle are connected when they subtend the same arc. These theorems lead to results about angles in the same segment, angles in a semicircle and cyclic quadrilaterals.

key_concepts.definition: Angles subtended by the same arc.
details: The angle at the centre of a circle is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
The theorem applies when both angles subtend the same arc. Check the intercepted arc and whether the vertices are on the same side before using it.

key_concepts.concept: Angles in the same segment and in a semicircle
key_concepts.definition: Special results for angles at the circumference.
details: Angles subtended by the same chord in the same segment are equal.
An angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference is a right angle ($90^\circ$). This is called the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem.

key_concepts.definition: Quadrilaterals with all four vertices on one circle.
details: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; each opposite pair sums to $180^\circ$.
An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.
Use the fact that all four vertices lie on the same circle; the result does not apply to an arbitrary quadrilateral.

worked_examples.problem: A central angle and an inscribed angle subtend the same arc. If the central angle is $116^\circ$, find the inscribed angle.
solution_steps: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc.
The inscribed angle is $116^\circ/2=58^\circ$.

worked_examples.problem: In cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, angle $A$ measures $105^\circ$. Find the opposite angle $C$.
solution_steps: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to $180^\circ$.
$105^\circ+m\angle C=180^\circ$.
Therefore $m\angle C=180^\circ-105^\circ=75^\circ$.

worked_examples.problem: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $C$ is a point on the circumference. If $\angle BAC=35^\circ$, find $\angle ABC$.
solution_steps: The angle subtended by diameter $AB$ at $C$ is $90^\circ$.
The angles of triangle $ABC$ sum to $180^\circ$.
So $35^\circ+90^\circ+m\angle ABC=180^\circ$, giving $m\angle ABC=55^\circ$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the central-angle theorem for angles that do not subtend the same arc.
common_mistakes.correction: Identify the common intercepted arc before applying the factor of 2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying the same-segment theorem to vertices in opposite segments.
common_mistakes.correction: Angles in the same segment are equal. Angles in opposite segments subtended by the same chord are supplementary.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming opposite angles of every quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees.
common_mistakes.correction: That property applies to cyclic quadrilaterals, where all four vertices lie on one circle.

quick_summary: The central angle is twice the inscribed angle subtending the same arc.
Angles in the same segment are equal.
An angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to $180^\circ$.

hs_math_t09_st12.title: Tangents and secants
hs_math_t09_st12.overview: Tangents touch a circle at one point, while secants intersect it at two points. Euclidean theorems connect tangent lengths, radius directions, chord angles and products of secant segments.

key_concepts.definition: The right angle at the point of contact.
details: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point.
The radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent.
A line perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint on the circle is a tangent at that point.

key_concepts.concept: Equal tangents from an external point
key_concepts.definition: Two tangent segments drawn from one point have equal lengths.
details: If $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from an external point $P$ to a circle, then $PA=PB$.
The two right triangles formed with the radii are congruent by RHS, which justifies the equality.

key_concepts.definition: An angle between a tangent and a chord.
details: The angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment of the circle.
Identify the chord and the opposite segment before equating the angles.

key_concepts.definition: Products of lengths measured from the same external point.
details: For a tangent $PT$ and secant $PAB$ from external point $P$, $PT^2=PA\times PB$, where $PA$ is the external part and $PB$ is the entire secant.
For two secants $PAB$ and $PCD$ from the same external point, $PA\times PB=PC\times PD$. In each product, multiply the external part by the full secant length.

variables.P: External point; PA and PB are tangent segments

worked_examples.problem: A tangent $PT$ and a secant $PAB$ are drawn from external point $P$. The external part $PA=4$ cm and the entire secant $PB=16$ cm. Find $PT$.
solution_steps: Use the tangent-secant theorem: $PT^2=PA\times PB$.
Take the positive square root because length is positive: $PT=8$ cm.

worked_examples.problem: Two tangents from an external point have lengths $3x+2$ cm and $5x-10$ cm. Find $x$ and the tangent length.
solution_steps: Tangents from the same external point are equal: $3x+2=5x-10$.
Rearrange: $12=2x$, so $x=6$.
Each tangent has length $3(6)+2=20$ cm.

worked_examples.problem: Two secants are drawn from $P$. Their external and total lengths are 3 cm and 12 cm for the first secant, and 4 cm and $x$ cm for the second. Find $x$.
solution_steps: By the secant-secant theorem, external part times whole secant is equal for the two secants.
$3\times12=4x$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the inner part instead of the whole secant length.
common_mistakes.correction: Multiply the external segment by the full secant length (external plus internal part). Do not multiply by the internal part alone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a tangent is perpendicular to every radius.
common_mistakes.correction: The tangent is perpendicular only to the radius drawn to its point of contact.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the alternate segment theorem with the wrong angle.
common_mistakes.correction: The chord must be the same, and the angle at the circumference must lie in the opposite (alternate) segment.

quick_summary: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Tangents from the same external point are equal.
The angle between a tangent and chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
For tangent-secant and secant-secant theorems, multiply external part by whole secant length.

hs_math_t09_st13.title: Geometric constructions
hs_math_t09_st13.overview: Ruler-and-compass constructions produce exact geometric figures without measuring their final angles or lengths directly. Every construction should include clear steps and a reason explaining why the resulting points, lines or angles have the required properties.

key_concepts.definition: Constructing equal distances and equal angles.
details: To construct a **perpendicular bisector** of segment $AB$, set the compass radius to more than half of $AB$. Draw arcs of the same radius from $A$ and $B$ so they intersect above and below the segment. Join the two arc intersections. Each intersection is equidistant from $A$ and $B$, so the joining line is the perpendicular bisector.

To construct an **angle bisector**, draw an arc centred at the vertex to mark equal-distance points on the two arms. From those two points draw equal-radius arcs that intersect inside the angle. Join the vertex to the arc intersection. The two resulting triangles are congruent, so the angles are equal.

key_concepts.definition: Constructing 60°, 30°, 90° and 45°.
details: A **60°** angle is constructed by using equal compass radii to form an equilateral triangle.
A **30°** angle is obtained by bisecting a constructed 60° angle.
A **90°** angle is constructed by erecting a perpendicular to a line. A **45°** angle is obtained by bisecting a 90° angle.

key_concepts.definition: Constructing from given measurements or angle conditions.
details: For an **SSS triangle**, draw the given base. Draw arcs from its endpoints with radii equal to the other two given sides. Their intersection gives the third vertex; join it to both endpoints.
For an **SAS triangle**, draw one given side, construct the included angle at one endpoint, mark the second given side on that ray, and join the final endpoints.
For an **ASA triangle**, draw the given included side, construct the two given base angles at its endpoints, and use the intersection of the rays as the third vertex.

To draw a line parallel to a given line through an external point, copy a corresponding angle made by a transversal at the given point. The converse of the corresponding-angle theorem justifies the parallel result.

key_concepts.definition: Constructing a tangent to a circle.
details: For a tangent at a known point $T$ on a circle with centre $O$, construct the line through $T$ perpendicular to radius $OT$. The radius-tangent theorem proves it is a tangent.

From an external point $P$, join $OP$ and construct its perpendicular bisector to locate midpoint $M$. Draw the circle with centre $M$ and radius $MO$; it meets the original circle at tangent points $T_1$ and $T_2$. Join $P$ to each point. Since $OP$ is a diameter of the auxiliary circle, $\angle OTP=90^\circ$, so each line is tangent.

worked_examples.problem: Describe how to construct a $45^\circ$ angle using only a compass and straightedge.
solution_steps: Construct a perpendicular to the given line at the chosen vertex to form a $90^\circ$ angle.
Use the angle-bisector construction on the $90^\circ$ angle: draw an arc from the vertex to meet both arms, then draw equal-radius arcs from those two intersection points.
Join the vertex to the intersection of the arcs. The two angles are equal, so each measures $90^\circ/2=45^\circ$.
worked_examples.final_answer: Construct a right angle and bisect it.

worked_examples.problem: Construct a triangle with side lengths 6 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. State why the construction is valid.
solution_steps: Draw a base segment $AB=6$ cm.
With centre $A$, draw an arc of radius 4 cm. With centre $B$, draw an arc of radius 5 cm.
Mark an intersection $C$ of the arcs and join $AC$ and $BC$.
By construction, $AC=4$ cm and $BC=5$ cm while $AB=6$ cm, so the triangle has the required three side lengths.
worked_examples.final_answer: $\triangle ABC$ with sides 6 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, constructed by SSS.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing the compass width while constructing equal arcs.
common_mistakes.correction: Keep the same compass radius whenever the construction requires equal distances.

common_mistakes.mistake: Joining the wrong arc intersection when constructing a triangle.
common_mistakes.correction: Choose one of the intersections of the two side-length arcs; either gives a valid reflected triangle on the opposite side of the base.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling a line parallel because it looks parallel.
common_mistakes.correction: Justify parallelism by the copied corresponding angle and the converse angle theorem.

quick_summary: Use equal-radius arcs to construct perpendicular and angle bisectors.
Construct 60° using an equilateral triangle; bisect to obtain 30° or 45°.
Construct triangles from SSS, SAS or ASA measurements.
Copy a corresponding angle to construct a parallel line.
A tangent at a circle point is perpendicular to the radius there.

hs_math_t09_st14.title: Pythagorean theorem and applications
hs_math_t09_st14.overview: The Pythagorean theorem relates the side lengths of a right-angled triangle. It can be used to find unknown sides, test whether a triangle is right-angled, recognise integer triples and solve practical problems involving right-angle geometry.

key_concepts.definition: The relationship between the legs and hypotenuse.
details: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse $c$ equals the sum of the squares of the two perpendicular legs $a$ and $b$.
The **converse** states that if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle.

key_concepts.concept: An accessible proof using similar triangles
key_concepts.definition: Why the theorem is true.
details: In right triangle $ABC$, let $\angle C=90^\circ$ and draw altitude $CD$ to hypotenuse $AB$. The two smaller triangles are similar to the original triangle.
From $\triangle ACD\sim\triangle ABC$, corresponding sides give $AC^2=AB\times AD$.
From $\triangle BCD\sim\triangle ABC$, corresponding sides give $BC^2=AB\times BD$.
Add the equations: $AC^2+BC^2=AB(AD+BD)=AB\times AB=AB^2$. Therefore $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

key_concepts.definition: Using the theorem in calculations.
details: To find the hypotenuse, use $c=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. To find a leg, rearrange: $a=\sqrt{c^2-b^2}$.
A **Pythagorean triple** is a set of positive integers satisfying the theorem, such as 3–4–5, 5–12–13 and 8–15–17. Any positive integer multiple of a triple is also a triple.

key_concepts.definition: Diagonals and shortest right-angle distances.
details: A ladder leaning against a vertical wall, a diagonal across a rectangular surface and the diagonal through a cuboid can all be modelled using right triangles.
For a cuboid with perpendicular dimensions $l$, $w$ and $h$, applying Pythagoras twice gives the space diagonal $d=\sqrt{l^2+w^2+h^2}$.
Check that the situation really forms a right angle before applying the theorem.

worked_examples.problem: A 13 m ladder leans against a wall. Its base is 5 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
solution_steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse (13 m); the ground distance is one leg (5 m).
Let the wall height be $h$. Then $h^2+5^2=13^2$.
$h^2=169-25=144$, so $h=12$ m. Use the positive value because it is a length.

worked_examples.problem: A rectangular box is 3 cm wide, 4 cm long and 12 cm high. Find its space diagonal.
solution_steps: Use $d=\sqrt{l^2+w^2+h^2}$.

worked_examples.problem: A triangle has side lengths 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm. Show that it is right-angled.
solution_steps: The longest side is 25 cm.
By the converse of the Pythagorean theorem, the angle opposite the 25 cm side is $90^\circ$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding the squares when finding a leg.
common_mistakes.correction: If the hypotenuse and one leg are known, subtract the leg square from the hypotenuse square before taking the square root.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying the theorem to any triangle.
common_mistakes.correction: The Pythagorean theorem applies only to right-angled triangles.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing a shorter side as the hypotenuse.
common_mistakes.correction: The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle and is the longest side.

quick_summary: In a right triangle, $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
Use the positive square root for a side length.
The converse tests whether a triangle is right-angled.
Common triples include 3–4–5 and 5–12–13.

hs_math_t09_st15.title: Geometric proof and reasoning
hs_math_t09_st15.overview: A Euclidean proof is a logically connected argument in which every statement follows from the given information, definitions, axioms or previously established theorems. Proof-writing should be used throughout geometry; this lesson consolidates the structure and reasoning methods.

key_concepts.definition: Statements linked to reasons.
details: State the **Given** information and the **To Prove** statement clearly.
In a two-column proof, each row contains a mathematical **statement** and a valid **reason**. Common reasons include definitions, given facts, angle theorems, congruence criteria and CPCTC.
Keep vertex correspondence clear and do not use a fact that has not yet been established.

key_concepts.definition: Different foundations for mathematical reasoning.
details: An **axiom** or **postulate** is accepted without proof within the chosen system.
A **definition** assigns a precise meaning to a mathematical term.
A **theorem** is a statement established by proof from axioms, definitions and previously proved results. A converse reverses the implication and must be justified separately.

key_concepts.definition: Two ways to organise a valid argument.
details: A **direct proof** starts from the givens and uses valid deductions to reach the statement to be proved.
A **proof by contradiction** assumes the negation of the required statement and derives a contradiction with an accepted fact or theorem. The original statement must then be true.
A diagram can help identify relationships, but visual appearance alone is never a valid reason. Use only given facts, markings and proved results.

worked_examples.problem: Given $AB=AC$ in triangle $ABC$, prove that $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$.
solution_steps: Draw the angle bisector $AD$ of $\angle BAC$, meeting $BC$ at $D$.
In triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$: $AB=AC$ (given); $\angle BAD=\angle DAC$ (construction); and $AD=AD$ (common side).
Therefore $\triangle ABD\cong\triangle ACD$ by SAS.
By CPCTC, $\angle ABD=\angle ACD$. Since $D$ lies on $BC$, these are $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ACB$.

worked_examples.problem: Prove by contradiction that a triangle cannot have two right angles.
solution_steps: Assume, for contradiction, that two interior angles of a triangle are each $90^\circ$.
Their sum is already $180^\circ$.
But the three interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$, so the third angle would have to be $0^\circ$.
Every interior angle of a non-degenerate triangle is positive. This is a contradiction.
worked_examples.final_answer: A triangle cannot have two right angles.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the appearance of a diagram as a reason.
common_mistakes.correction: Use only information stated in the givens, marked in the diagram or established by a theorem.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing a statement without a reason.
common_mistakes.correction: Every line in a two-column proof must be justified by a given fact, definition, axiom, postulate or theorem.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a converse is automatically true.
common_mistakes.correction: A converse reverses the hypothesis and conclusion. Use it only when that converse has been established as a valid theorem.

quick_summary: A proof is a chain of statements, each with a valid reason.
Use definitions, axioms, givens and established theorems.
Prove triangle congruence before using CPCTC.
In contradiction, assume the opposite and derive an impossibility.
